EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

================================================================  
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (static and dynamic/event-study versions) combined with a Bartik (shift-share) instrument for continuous “price-shock exposure.”

Why it fits:  
• The Brazilian liberalisation generated large tariff cuts that differed sharply by 5-digit industry but were legislated centrally and pre-announced.  
• These tariff cuts map mechanically into domestic sectoral price changes, but pass-through may be incomplete or endogenous. A Bartik instrument—tariff change × worker’s pre-reform sector weights—provides plausibly exogenous exposure and lets us scale effects continuously, not only “treated vs. control.”  
• RAIS gives us a long worker panel (1986–2005) so we can compare pre- and post-reform trends, estimate dynamic adjustment paths, and include individual fixed effects.  

Estimation sequence  
(a) First-stage: instrument the realised log sectoral value-added deflator Pst with the legislated tariff schedule τst.  
(b) Reduced form / DiD: regress worker outcomes on the interacted tariff/price exposure, with worker and year FE, and plot event-time coefficients to trace adjustment.  

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable  
Continuous: Exposurei ≡ Σs θis,pre × Δτs,88-94 (where θis,pre is the fraction of worker i’s employment in sector s over 1986–1988; Δτs is the cumulative tariff change in s).  
For some presentations we will dichotomise: Treated = 1 if Exposurei is in the top quartile of the absolute tariff fall distribution; Control = bottom quartile.

Timing  
t = 0 is 1991, the mid-point of the reform. We estimate τ = −5,…,+12 relative to 1991 and omit τ = −1 as baseline.  

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Parallel trends: absent tariff cuts, outcomes of high- and low-exposure workers would have evolved in parallel. Plausibility: macro shocks hit all workers; we can test pre-trends graphically/in regression.  
A2. Exogeneity of tariff schedule: post-1988 tariff path was set politically, not by plant-level shocks. The literature treats these reforms as exogenous to future, worker-level outcomes.  
A3. No anticipatory re-sorting that fully adjusts before 1988. We can check by testing for large sectoral mobility 1986–1988 correlated with Δτs.  
A4. Stable unit treatment value (no general-equilibrium contamination across workers with different exposure). Given Brazil’s size and that exposure is a share-weighted individual statistic, partial equilibrium is a reasonable approximation for micro outcomes; we address macro feedbacks by including year FE and sector*year controls.  
A5. First-stage relevance: tariff changes substantially predict within-sector price movements. We can verify F-stat > 10 in the first stage.  

4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Simultaneous policies (privatisations, Real Plan 1994).  
Fix: add state-year FE, control for sector-specific privatisation dummies, and include a macro stabilisation dummy.  

T2. Selective worker mobility (sorting into booming sectors).  
Fix: (i) baseline sector weights are frozen at 1986–1988, so the treatment is predetermined; (ii) include individual FE so identification comes from within-worker time variation in exposure arising from price changes, not from switching sectors.  

T3. Measurement error in sectoral prices.  
Fix: use tariff schedule as an IV; also re-run using world-price changes as an alternative instrument.  

5. R CODE OUTLINE  
----------------------------------------------------------------  

```r
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dim FE regressions
library(did)         # for event-study plots
library(modelsummary)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
# --------------------------------------------------------------
rais <- fread("RAIS_1986_2005_1pct.csv")          # worker panel
tar  <- fread("Tariffs_1988_1994_by5dig.csv")     # sectoral tariffs
price<- fread("VAdeflators_1986_2005.csv")        # NA price indices

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct pre-reform sector weights (θ_i,s)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
pre_period <- rais[year %between% c(1986,1988)]
pre_weights <- pre_period[, .N, by=.(worker_id, sector5)]
pre_weights[, theta := N / sum(N), by = worker_id]
pre_weights <- pre_weights[, .(worker_id, sector5, theta)]

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Merge tariffs → sector shocks
# --------------------------------------------------------------
tar[, d_tau := log(tariff_1994 + 1) - log(tariff_1988 + 1)]

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Build worker-level exposure
# --------------------------------------------------------------
exposure <- merge(pre_weights, tar[, .(sector5, d_tau)], by="sector5")
exposure <- exposure[, .(tariff_shock = sum(theta * d_tau)), by=worker_id]

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Assemble analysis panel
# --------------------------------------------------------------
panel <- merge(rais, exposure, by="worker_id")
panel <- merge(panel, price, by=c("sector5","year"), suffixes=c("", "_sect"))

# Key variables
panel[, logw := log(hourly_wage_deflated)]
panel[, post  := as.integer(year >= 1991)]

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. DiD main spec  (continuous exposure × post)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
panel[, treat_post := tariff_shock * post]

est_main <- feols(logw ~ treat_post | worker_id + year, data = panel,
                  cluster = ~sector5)
etable(est_main, dict=c(treat_post="Shock × Post"), se="cluster")

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Dynamic event-study (Callaway–Sant’Anna)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# Create cohort = first year with positive exposure (all 1991)
panel[, cohort := 1991]
cs_results <- att_gt(yname="logw",
                     tname="year",
                     idname="worker_id",
                     gname="cohort",
                     xformla=~tariff_shock,
                     data=panel)
ggdid(cs_results)  # dynamic graph

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. Robustness: placebo pre-period (1986–1990 only)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
panel_placebo <- panel[year < 1991]
panel_placebo[, placebo := tariff_shock * (year >= 1988)]
est_placebo <- feols(logw ~ placebo | worker_id + year,
                     data = panel_placebo,
                     cluster = ~sector5)
etable(est_main, est_placebo, se="cluster",
       dict=c(placebo="Shock × FakePost"))
```

6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
• Wages: Workers with larger negative tariff shocks in their baseline sector (import-competing) will experience relative wage losses of roughly 4–6 log-points in the short run (2–3 years) and 8–10 log-points after a decade if they stay.  
• Reallocation: Half-life of about 6 years—50 % of the employment gap between treated and control sectors will close by 2000.  
• Welfare distribution: Low-educated males benefit from the expansion of Agriculture/Mining; older, higher-educated workers in High-Tech Manufacturing lose the most.  

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DiD/Bartik)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: Strong first stage (F > 10) ………………… 1  
C2: Pre-trends parallel visually & statistically … 0.8  
C3: No large anticipatory sorting ………………… 0.7  
C4: No concurrent sector-specific shocks ……… 0.6  
C5: SUTVA/limited GE spillovers ………………… 0.6  
Overall ≈ 3.7 / 5.  

================================================================  
This plan delivers causal estimates of the incidence, timing, and distribution of labour-market adjustment to Brazil’s trade shocks and provides a platform to simulate alternative policies (re-training grants, mobility subsidies) by inserting them into the second-stage structural model of sector choice.
